paras: The whipping of Ed Williams was a mob assault in Augusta, Kentucky, in November 1903, in which a group of local residents took Williams, a Black man, from the town jail at night and whipped him. He was accused of "impudence to young white ladies," and he left Augusta afterward. The only known report, a short item in the Maysville Daily Public Ledger, called the whipping "much-deserved."

According to the Ledger, Williams had recently been held in the Maysville jail, "charged with raping a Dover colored girl." The item does not say how that charge was resolved or why he was in the Augusta jail when the mob came.

A few nights before 20 November 1903, men the paper called "Augusta citizens" took Williams from the jail at Augusta and whipped him. The stated reason was his "impudence to young white ladies"; the item gives no names, numbers, or details of the women or of the whipping itself.

After the whipping Williams left Augusta, or in the Ledger's words, "he skipped that town." No report of arrests, an investigation, or any official response to the removal of a prisoner from the jail was found.

The Daily Public Ledger of Maysville carried the story on 20 November 1903 as one paragraph in a front-page column of local notes, between a funeral notice and a lawsuit over sandwiches. The paper took the attackers' side, describing the whipping as "much-deserved" and as Williams's "punishment," and it linked him to the earlier rape charge. No other white paper and no Black newspaper is known to have reported the incident.
